question: Let (G, .) and (H, *) be groups with identities e_G and e_H, and let phi: G -> H be a group homomorphism, meaning phi(x.y) = phi(x)*phi(y) for all x, y in G. Prove from the homomorphism property alone (without assuming phi is injective, surjective, or that G or H is finite) that phi(e_G) = e_H and that phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1} for every g in G. State explicitly which group axioms (uniqueness of identity, uniqueness of inverses, cancellation) you invoke at each step, and explain why these two facts justify the standing claims that every representation phi satisfies phi(e) = 1_V and phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}.
reference_answer: For the identity: pick any g in G and write g = e_G . g, so phi(g) = phi(e_G . g) = phi(e_G) * phi(g). Thus phi(e_G) * phi(g) = phi(g) = e_H * phi(g). Right-multiplying both sides by phi(g)^{-1} in H (which exists because H is a group) and cancelling gives phi(e_G) = e_H; equivalently, phi(e_G) acts as a left identity on phi(g), and since the identity of H is unique, phi(e_G) = e_H. For the inverse: fix g in G. Then e_H = phi(e_G) = phi(g . g^{-1}) = phi(g) * phi(g^{-1}), and likewise e_H = phi(g^{-1} . g) = phi(g^{-1}) * phi(g). So phi(g^{-1}) is a two-sided inverse of phi(g) in H; because inverses in a group are unique, phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}. The only axioms used are the homomorphism identity, the group axioms e_G . g = g and g . g^{-1} = g^{-1} . g = e_G in G, existence of inverses in H (to cancel), and uniqueness of the identity and of inverses in H. Applied to a representation phi: G -> GL(V) with H = GL(V) and identity 1_V, these say precisely phi(e) = 1_V and phi(g^{-1}) = phi(g)^{-1}; in particular every phi(g) is automatically invertible with the stated inverse, so invertibility need not be postulated separately.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and let <.|.> be any inner product on V. Define the averaged form <v|w>_G := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>. Prove that (a) <.|.>_G is again an inner product on V; (b) every phi(g) is unitary with respect to <.|.>_G, i.e. <phi(g) v | phi(g) w>_G = <v|w>_G; and (c) consequently, for any G-invariant subspace W, its orthogonal complement W^perp taken with respect to <.|.>_G is also G-invariant, so that V = W (+) W^perp as representations. Explain exactly where the ability to average over G is used.
reference_answer: (a) Each summand <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> is sesquilinear in (v,w) because phi(g) is linear and <.|.> is sesquilinear, and a finite average of sesquilinear forms is sesquilinear; Hermitian symmetry is inherited termwise. For positivity, <v|v>_G = (1/|G|) sum_g <phi(g)v | phi(g)v> >= 0 as an average of nonnegative terms, and it vanishes only if every term is 0; the g = e term gives <v|v> = 0, hence v = 0 since <.|.> is definite. So <.|.>_G is a genuine inner product. (b) Fix h in G. Then <phi(h)v | phi(h)w>_G = (1/|G|) sum_g <phi(g)phi(h)v | phi(g)phi(h)w> = (1/|G|) sum_g <phi(gh)v | phi(gh)w> by the homomorphism property. As g ranges over G so does g' = gh (left translation is a bijection of G), so the sum equals <v|w>_G. Thus phi(h) preserves <.|.>_G and is unitary for it. (c) Let W be G-invariant and u in W^perp. For any g and w in W, <phi(g)u | w>_G = <u | phi(g)^* w>_G = <u | phi(g^{-1}) w>_G, using that the adjoint of the <.|.>_G-unitary phi(g) is phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g^{-1}). Invariance gives phi(g^{-1}) w in W, so the pairing is 0; hence phi(g)u in W^perp and W^perp is invariant. Then V = W (+) W^perp (nondegeneracy) with both summands invariant, a decomposition of representations. The averaging over G is used exactly twice: forming the normalized sum (1/|G|) sum_g requires it to be finite (compact groups replace it by Haar integration), and the reindexing g -> gh being a bijection is what makes the form G-invariant.

question: Let (phi, V) be a representation of a finite group G over a field whose characteristic does not divide |G|, and let W be a G-invariant subspace with some (not necessarily invariant) projection P_W onto W (P_W^2 = P_W, im P_W = W). Define Q_W := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1}. Prove that Q_W commutes with every phi(g), that im Q_W = W and Q_W is a projection, and conclude that ker Q_W is a G-invariant complement, so V = W (+) ker Q_W as representations. Indicate where the hypothesis on the characteristic is used.
reference_answer: Equivariance: for h in G, phi(h) Q_W phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(h)phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1} phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(hg) P_W phi(hg)^{-1}. Reindexing g' = hg (a bijection of G) shows this equals Q_W, so phi(h) Q_W = Q_W phi(h) for all h. Image in W: invariance means phi(g)^{-1} maps V into V, P_W maps into W, and phi(g) maps W into W, so each term phi(g) P_W phi(g)^{-1} has image in W; the average does too, giving im Q_W subset W. Q_W fixes W pointwise: for w in W, phi(g)^{-1} w in W, P_W fixes it, and phi(g) phi(g)^{-1} w = w, so each term returns w; the normalized average (1/|G|) sum_g w = w. This normalization is exactly where the characteristic hypothesis enters: 1/|G| must exist in the field, i.e. |G| must be invertible, which holds iff the characteristic does not divide |G|. Hence Q_W|_W = id_W, so Q_W maps everything into W and acts as the identity there, giving Q_W^2 = Q_W: a projection onto W. Finally, since Q_W commutes with all phi(g), both im Q_W = W and ker Q_W are G-invariant, and V = im Q_W (+) ker Q_W = W (+) ker Q_W. Thus W has a G-invariant complement and the decomposition is of representations.

question: Let (phi_1, V_1) and (phi_2, V_2) be irreducible representations of a group G and let f: V_1 -> V_2 be G-equivariant, meaning f . phi_1(g) = phi_2(g) . f for all g in G. Prove that either f = 0 or f is an isomorphism (so V_1 ~ V_2). Your proof must show that ker f is a G-invariant subspace of V_1 and that im f is a G-invariant subspace of V_2, and then use irreducibility to force the conclusion.
reference_answer: ker f is G-invariant: take v in ker f and g in G. Then f(phi_1(g) v) = phi_2(g)(f(v)) = phi_2(g)(0) = 0, using equivariance and f(v) = 0; so phi_1(g) v in ker f. Since V_1 is irreducible, its only invariant subspaces are {0} and V_1, so either ker f = V_1 (f = 0) or ker f = {0} (f injective). im f is G-invariant: any element of im f is f(v), and phi_2(g)(f(v)) = f(phi_1(g) v) in im f by equivariance, so phi_2(g) maps im f into im f. Irreducibility of V_2 forces im f = {0} or im f = V_2. If f is not the zero map, then ker f = {0} (injective) and im f is not {0}, hence im f = V_2 (surjective). An injective and surjective linear map is a bijection, i.e. a vector-space isomorphism; it intertwines phi_1 and phi_2, so it is an isomorphism of representations and V_1 ~ V_2. Therefore f = 0 or f is an isomorphism, with no middle case. The only properties used are equivariance (invariance of kernel and image) and irreducibility (no nontrivial invariant subspaces); no field assumption is needed for this part.

question: Let (phi, V) be an irreducible representation of a group G on a finite-dimensional vector space V over an algebraically closed field F (for example F = C), and let f: V -> V be G-equivariant, i.e. f . phi(g) = phi(g) . f for all g. Prove that f = lambda . 1_V for some scalar lambda in F. Make explicit where algebraic closure and finite dimension are used, and derive as a corollary that any operator X commuting with an irreducible representation is a scalar multiple of the identity.
reference_answer: Because F is algebraically closed and V is finite-dimensional, the characteristic polynomial of f has a root in F, so f has an eigenvalue lambda in F; this is exactly where both hypotheses are needed (over R or in infinite dimension an operator may have no eigenvalue). Set f' := f - lambda . 1_V. Since 1_V commutes with every phi(g) and f is equivariant, f' phi(g) = f phi(g) - lambda phi(g) = phi(g) f - lambda phi(g) = phi(g) f', so f' is G-equivariant. Moreover f' is not invertible: lambda is an eigenvalue, so some nonzero v has (f - lambda)v = 0, giving ker f' != {0}. By part (i) of Schur's Lemma applied to the equivariant endomorphism f' on the irreducible V, f' is either zero or an isomorphism; being non-invertible, it must be zero. Hence f = lambda . 1_V. Corollary: if X satisfies phi(g) X = X phi(g) for all g, then X is a G-equivariant endomorphism of the irreducible V, so X = lambda . 1_V for some lambda; i.e. the commutant of an irreducible representation consists only of scalar multiples of the identity.

question: Let G be an abelian group. Prove that every complex irreducible representation (phi, V) of G is one-dimensional. You may use Schur's Lemma. Make clear exactly where commutativity of G and where the complex (algebraically closed) field are used, and explain why the statement can fail if the field is not algebraically closed.
reference_answer: Fix h in G. Because G is abelian, for every g in G, phi(g) phi(h) = phi(gh) = phi(hg) = phi(h) phi(g); thus the single operator phi(h) commutes with every phi(g), so phi(h) is a G-equivariant endomorphism of V. Since V is irreducible and the field is C (algebraically closed), Schur (ii) gives phi(h) = lambda_h . 1_V for some lambda_h in C. This holds for every h in G, so every representation operator is a scalar multiple of the identity. Hence for any nonzero v in V and any h, phi(h) v = lambda_h v lies in span(v), so span(v) is a G-invariant subspace. By irreducibility the only nonzero invariant subspace is V, so V = span(v) is one-dimensional. Commutativity is used to make each phi(h) commute with all phi(g) (so Schur applies to phi(h) itself); algebraic closure is used in Schur (ii) to turn phi(h) into a genuine scalar. Over a non-algebraically-closed field the conclusion fails: a generic rotation representation of a cyclic group on R^2 is irreducible over R (a non-trivial rotation has no real eigenvector, hence no proper real invariant subspace) yet is two-dimensional, precisely because the rotation operator is not a real scalar.

question: Let rho be any single-qubit density matrix (a 2x2 positive semidefinite operator with trace 1). Using the fact that the Pauli operators {1, X, Y, Z} generate an irreducible representation of the single-qubit Pauli group acting on C^2, prove that (1/4)(rho + X rho X + Y rho Y + Z rho Z) = (1/2) 1. Base your argument on Schur's Lemma / the commutant-is-scalars corollary and on the trace, not on a brute-force coordinate computation.
reference_answer: Write T(rho) := (1/4)(rho + X rho X + Y rho Y + Z rho Z); each P in {1,X,Y,Z} is Hermitian and unitary, so P rho P^dagger = P rho P. Claim: T(rho) commutes with the Pauli representation. It suffices to check commutation with each generator Q in {X,Y,Z}. Conjugating, Q T(rho) Q = (1/4) sum_P (QP) rho (QP), and as P ranges over {1,X,Y,Z} the products QP range over {1,X,Y,Z} up to overall phases (Pauli-group multiplication permutes the four classes). Since P rho P^dagger is insensitive to a global phase on P (phases cancel between P and P^dagger), the multiset {QP rho (QP)^dagger} equals {P rho P}, so Q T(rho) Q = T(rho), i.e. Q T(rho) = T(rho) Q. Thus T(rho) commutes with the generators, hence with the whole irreducible Pauli representation on C^2. By the Schur commutant corollary (commutant of an irrep = scalars), T(rho) = lambda . 1. Fix lambda by the trace: tr T(rho) = (1/4)(tr rho + tr(X rho X) + tr(Y rho Y) + tr(Z rho Z)) = (1/4)(1+1+1+1) = 1, using cyclicity and P^2 = 1 so tr(P rho P) = tr(rho) = 1. Also tr(lambda 1) = 2 lambda, so 2 lambda = 1, lambda = 1/2. Therefore T(rho) = (1/2) 1, the maximally mixed state. The argument used only irreducibility (via Schur) and trace normalization, not the entries of rho - which is the content of the symmetrization principle.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional representation of a group G and define its character by chi(g) := tr(phi(g)). Prove that (a) chi is a class function, i.e. chi(h g h^{-1}) = chi(g) for all g, h in G, and (b) chi(e) = dim V. State precisely which properties of the trace and which property of phi you use, and explain why being a class function means chi is really a function on conjugacy classes.
reference_answer: (a) Fix g, h in G. Using multiplicativity of phi, phi(h g h^{-1}) = phi(h) phi(g) phi(h^{-1}) = phi(h) phi(g) phi(h)^{-1}, the last equality from phi(h^{-1}) = phi(h)^{-1} (valid for any representation). Apply the trace: chi(h g h^{-1}) = tr(phi(h) phi(g) phi(h)^{-1}). By cyclicity of the trace, tr(A B A^{-1}) = tr(A^{-1} A B) = tr(B) with A = phi(h), B = phi(g), so this equals tr(phi(g)) = chi(g). Hence chi is constant on each conjugacy class {h g h^{-1} : h in G}, i.e. a class function; equivalently chi descends to a well-defined function on the set of conjugacy classes of G. The trace properties used are linearity (to define tr) and cyclicity tr(AB) = tr(BA); the property of phi used is multiplicativity phi(xy) = phi(x)phi(y) together with phi(h^{-1}) = phi(h)^{-1}. (b) Since phi(e) = 1_V (a representation sends the identity to the identity operator), chi(e) = tr(1_V) = dim V, as the trace of the identity on an n-dimensional space is n. question: Let G be a finite group and let the characters of its pairwise inequivalent complex irreducible representations W_1, ..., W_k be chi_1, ..., chi_k, orthonormal for the inner product (x, y) = (1/|G|) sum_{g} conj(x(g)) y(g); so (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij}. Let (phi, V) be an arbitrary finite-dimensional complex representation with isotypical decomposition V ~ (+)_i W_i^{(+) n_i} (n_i the multiplicity of W_i). Prove that n_i = (chi_i, chi_V), where chi_V is the character of V. Then prove the two consequences: V is irreducible iff (chi_V, chi_V) = 1, and two representations are isomorphic iff they have equal characters.
reference_answer: By additivity of the character under direct sums (chi_{A (+) B} = chi_A + chi_B, which follows from tr being additive on block-diagonal operators), the isotypical decomposition V ~ (+)_j W_j^{(+) n_j} gives chi_V = sum_j n_j chi_j. Taking the inner product with chi_i and using bilinearity (conjugate-linearity in the first slot but the n_j are real nonnegative integers) together with orthonormality, (chi_i, chi_V) = (chi_i, sum_j n_j chi_j) = sum_j n_j (chi_i, chi_j) = sum_j n_j delta_{ij} = n_i. This proves the multiplicity formula. Consequence 1: compute (chi_V, chi_V) = (sum_i n_i chi_i, sum_j n_j chi_j) = sum_{i,j} n_i n_j delta_{ij} = sum_i n_i^2. Since the n_i are nonnegative integers, sum_i n_i^2 = 1 holds iff exactly one n_i equals 1 and all others are 0, i.e. iff V is (isomorphic to) a single irreducible W_i; thus V is irreducible iff (chi_V, chi_V) = 1. Consequence 2: if V ~ V' then they have the same character (characters are isomorphism invariants, since conjugate representation matrices have equal trace). Conversely, the multiplicities n_i = (chi_i, chi_V) are determined entirely by chi_V; so if chi_V = chi_{V'} then n_i(V) = n_i(V') for all i, meaning V and V' have the same isotypical decomposition and hence V ~ V'. Therefore two representations are isomorphic iff their characters coincide.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G, and for X in L(V) define the symmetrized operator Xbar := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that Xbar is G-invariant, i.e. phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h) for all h in G. (b) Using Schur's Lemma, prove that if V = W_1 (+) W_2 is a multiplicity-free decomposition into two inequivalent irreducibles, then in a basis adapted to W_1, W_2 the operator Xbar is block diagonal with each diagonal block a scalar multiple of the identity, and the off-diagonal blocks vanish. Explain which part of Schur kills the off-diagonal blocks and which part scalarizes the diagonal blocks.
reference_answer: (a) For h in G, phi(h) Xbar phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(h)phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1}phi(h)^{-1} = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(hg) X phi(hg)^{-1}. Reindexing g' = hg (a bijection of G) leaves the average unchanged, so phi(h) Xbar phi(h)^{-1} = Xbar, i.e. phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h). Thus Xbar commutes with the whole representation; it is G-equivariant. (b) Write Xbar in block form with respect to V = W_1 (+) W_2: Xbar = [[A_{11}, A_{12}], [A_{21}, A_{22}]], where A_{ij}: W_j -> W_i. Equivariance phi(h) Xbar = Xbar phi(h) restricted to blocks says A_{ij} phi_j(h) = phi_i(h) A_{ij} for all h, i.e. each A_{ij} is an intertwiner from the irreducible W_j to the irreducible W_i. For the off-diagonal blocks i != j: W_1 and W_2 are inequivalent irreducibles, so by Schur part (i) any intertwiner between them is zero; hence A_{12} = 0 and A_{21} = 0. For the diagonal blocks i = j: A_{ii} is an equivariant endomorphism of the irreducible W_i over C, so by Schur part (ii) A_{ii} = lambda_i . 1_{W_i} for some scalar lambda_i. Therefore Xbar = lambda_1 1_{W_1} (+) lambda_2 1_{W_2}, block diagonal with scalar blocks. Part (i) of Schur kills the off-diagonal blocks (maps between inequivalent irreps), and part (ii) scalarizes the diagonal blocks (equivariant endomorphisms of an irrep). This is exactly the small multiplicity-free instance of the general symmetrization result; with multiplicities the diagonal blocks would instead be 1_{W_k} tensored with an arbitrary operator on the multiplicity space.

question: Let (phi, V) be a representation of a group G and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V with the swap operator F defined by F(|x> (x) |y>) = |y> (x) |x>, extended linearly. (a) Prove F^2 = 1 and that F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g. (b) Define Pi_sym := (1/2)(1 + F) and Pi_asym := (1/2)(1 - F). Prove that Pi_sym and Pi_asym are orthogonal projections with Pi_sym + Pi_asym = 1 and Pi_sym Pi_asym = 0, that their images are exactly the +1 and -1 eigenspaces of F, and that both images are G-invariant subspaces, giving V (x) V = Sym^2(V) (+) Lambda^2(V) as representations.
reference_answer: (a) On product vectors F(F(|x> (x) |y>)) = F(|y> (x) |x>) = |x> (x) |y>, so F^2 = 1 on a spanning set, hence everywhere by linearity; in particular F is an involution, so its only possible eigenvalues are +1 and -1. For commutation, (phi(g) (x) phi(g)) F (|x> (x) |y>) = (phi(g) (x) phi(g))(|y> (x) |x>) = phi(g)|y> (x) phi(g)|x> = F(phi(g)|x> (x) phi(g)|y>) = F (phi(g) (x) phi(g)) (|x> (x) |y>), and by linearity F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g. (b) Compute Pi_sym^2 = (1/4)(1 + F)^2 = (1/4)(1 + 2F + F^2) = (1/4)(2 + 2F) = (1/2)(1 + F) = Pi_sym, so Pi_sym is idempotent; similarly Pi_asym^2 = (1/4)(1 - 2F + F^2) = Pi_asym. Both are Hermitian since F is Hermitian (F = F^dagger because F is a real symmetric permutation / an involution that is also unitary, hence self-adjoint), so they are orthogonal projections. Pi_sym + Pi_asym = (1/2)(1 + F) + (1/2)(1 - F) = 1 and Pi_sym Pi_asym = (1/4)(1 + F)(1 - F) = (1/4)(1 - F^2) = (1/4)(1 - 1) = 0. Because Pi_sym Pi_asym = 0 and they sum to 1, their images are complementary. The image of Pi_sym is {|z> : F|z> = |z>} (the +1 eigenspace): if F|z> = |z> then Pi_sym|z> = |z>, and conversely any |z> in the image satisfies F|z> = F Pi_sym |z> = (1/2)(F + F^2)|z> = (1/2)(F + 1)|z> = Pi_sym|z> = |z>; likewise im Pi_asym is the -1 eigenspace. Finally, since F commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g), so do Pi_sym and Pi_asym (they are polynomials in F), hence their images are G-invariant subspaces. Therefore V (x) V = im Pi_sym (+) im Pi_asym = Sym^2(V) (+) Lambda^2(V) as representations.

question: Let (phi, V) be a finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group G. For the trivial representation, define P := (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} phi(g). Prove that (a) P is idempotent (P^2 = P), (b) im P = V^G := {|v> : phi(g)|v> = |v> for all g}, and (c) P commutes with every phi(h). Then explain, by taking the trace, why tr P equals the multiplicity of the trivial representation in V (the number of independent G-invariant vectors), connecting to the general character-projection formula P_W = (dim W / |G|) sum_g conj(chi_W(g)) phi(g).
reference_answer: (a) and (c) together: for any h in G, phi(h) P = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(h)phi(g) = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(hg) = (1/|G|) sum_{g'} phi(g') = P, reindexing g' = hg (a bijection of G); likewise P phi(h) = P by reindexing on the right. So phi(h) P = P = P phi(h) for all h, which gives both that P commutes with every phi(h) and that P is left/right absorbing for the group action. Idempotency follows: P^2 = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) P = (1/|G|) sum_g P = P, using phi(g) P = P from the previous line. (b) If |v> in im P, write |v> = P|w>; then phi(h)|v> = phi(h) P|w> = P|w> = |v> for all h, so |v> in V^G, giving im P subset V^G. Conversely if |v> in V^G then phi(g)|v> = |v> for all g, so P|v> = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g)|v> = (1/|G|) sum_g |v> = |v>, hence |v> in im P; thus V^G subset im P. Therefore im P = V^G. (b continued, trace) Since P is idempotent and (being an average of the unitaries phi(g) in a suitable invariant inner product) an orthogonal projection, its trace equals the dimension of its image: tr P = dim im P = dim V^G, which is precisely the number of independent G-invariant vectors, i.e. the multiplicity of the trivial representation in V. This is the chi_W = chi_triv = 1 case of the general formula P_W = (dim W/|G|) sum_g conj(chi_W(g)) phi(g): the trivial representation has dimension 1 and character identically 1, so P_triv = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) = P, and its trace recovers the multiplicity, consistent with the character inner-product formula for multiplicities.

question: A student claims: for any representation (phi, V) of a finite group G and any X in L(V), the symmetrized operator Xbar = (1/|G|) sum_g phi(g) X phi(g)^{-1} is always block diagonal with respect to the isotypical decomposition AND each diagonal block is a scalar multiple of the identity. Decide whether the second half of this claim is true in general. Give an explicit counterexample using the action of S_2 = {e, (12)} on (C^2)^{(x)2} by permuting the two tensor factors (so phi((12)) = F, the swap), and explain precisely what feature of the decomposition makes the diagonal block fail to be scalar.
reference_answer: The block-diagonal part of the claim is correct, but the assertion that every diagonal block is a scalar multiple of the identity is FALSE in general; it holds only when each isotypical component is a single copy of an irrep (multiplicity one). Counterexample: let S_2 act on (C^2)^{(x)2} by phi(e) = 1 and phi((12)) = F (swap). The isotypical decomposition is (C^2)^{(x)2} = Vtriv (+) Vsgn, where Vtriv is the 3-dimensional +1 eigenspace of F (symmetric subspace, spanned by |00>, |11>, (|01>+|10>)/sqrt 2) carrying three copies of the trivial irrep, and Vsgn is the 1-dimensional -1 eigenspace (spanned by (|01>-|10>)/sqrt 2) carrying the sign irrep. Now take X = |00><11| (a rank-one operator). Symmetrizing: Xbar = (1/2)(X + F X F^{-1}) = (1/2)(|00><11| + F|00><11|F) = (1/2)(|00><11| + |00><11|) = |00><11|, because F|00> = |00> and F|11> = |11> (both symmetric), so F X F = X. The operator Xbar = |00><11| maps entirely within the symmetric (trivial-isotypical) subspace Vtriv, so it is block diagonal (its Vsgn block and the off-diagonal blocks are zero, consistent with Schur part (i)). However, restricted to the 3-dimensional Vtriv it is the rank-one operator |00><11|, which is NOT a scalar multiple of the 3x3 identity (it is not even diagonal in the symmetric basis and has rank 1, trace 0). The reason the diagonal block is not scalar is multiplicity: Vtriv contains the trivial irrep three times, so Hom_G(triv, Vtriv) is 3-dimensional and the symmetrized operator restricted to Vtriv is of the form 1_{W_triv} (x) X_triv with X_triv an arbitrary 3x3 operator on the multiplicity space C^3 - only this multiplicity-space factor is scalar when the multiplicity is 1. Hence Schur's Lemma forces scalar diagonal blocks only in the multiplicity-free case; with multiplicity greater than 1 the diagonal block is merely of the form (identity on the irrep) (x) (arbitrary operator on the multiplicity space).

question: A student asserts: the tensor product of two irreducible representations of a group G is again irreducible. Show this is false by a counterexample. Specifically, take any representation (phi, V) of G with dim V >= 2 (you may take V irreducible) and consider the tensor-square representation on V (x) V. Exhibit a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V, and compute the dimensions to show V (x) V cannot be irreducible when dim V >= 2.
reference_answer: The claim is false. Let (phi, V) be any representation with d := dim V >= 2 (e.g. an irreducible one such as the standard representation of S_3 of dimension 2). Consider the tensor-square representation (phi (x) phi) on V (x) V, which has dimension d^2 >= 4. The swap operator F on V (x) V, defined by F(|x> (x) |y>) = |y> (x) |x>, commutes with phi(g) (x) phi(g) for all g (shown by swapping tensor factors), and F^2 = 1. Hence the +1 eigenspace Sym^2(V) and the -1 eigenspace Lambda^2(V) of F are both G-invariant subspaces of V (x) V, and V (x) V = Sym^2(V) (+) Lambda^2(V) as representations. Their dimensions are dim Sym^2(V) = d(d+1)/2 and dim Lambda^2(V) = d(d-1)/2 (standard counts of symmetric and antisymmetric index pairs). For d >= 2 both of these are strictly positive: dim Lambda^2(V) = d(d-1)/2 >= 1 and dim Sym^2(V) = d(d+1)/2 >= 3, and both are strictly less than d^2 (since each is a proper summand of a direct sum of two nonzero spaces). Thus Lambda^2(V) is a proper nonzero G-invariant subspace of V (x) V (and so is Sym^2(V)); the existence of such a subspace means V (x) V is reducible. Therefore even when V is irreducible, V (x) V fails to be irreducible as soon as dim V >= 2, refuting the claim. (For the degenerate case d = 1, Lambda^2(V) = 0 and V (x) V ~ V is one-dimensional hence irreducible, which is exactly why the hypothesis dim V >= 2 is needed.)

question: Proposition 3.22 says the decomposition of a representation into isotypical components is unique. A student over-reads this as: 'the decomposition of a representation into irreducible subrepresentations is unique.' Show by counterexample that the finer decomposition into individual irreducible subspaces is NOT unique, even though the isotypical components are. Use the trivial-isotypical component of the S_2 action on (C^2)^{(x)2} (equivalently, any space carrying the trivial representation with multiplicity >= 2) and exhibit two genuinely different splittings into irreducible lines.
reference_answer: The student's reading is wrong: it is the isotypical components that are unique, not the splitting of a multiplicity-greater-than-one component into individual irreducible subspaces. Take the S_2 action on (C^2)^{(x)2} with phi((12)) = F. The symmetric subspace Vtriv = Sym^2(C^2) is the +1 eigenspace of F, a 3-dimensional space on which S_2 acts trivially; it is the trivial-isotypical component and is uniquely determined (it equals the +1 eigenspace of F, basis-independent). But because S_2 acts as the identity on all of Vtriv, EVERY one-dimensional subspace of Vtriv is an irreducible (trivial) subrepresentation, and Vtriv can be written as a direct sum of three trivial lines in infinitely many ways. Concretely, one splitting is Vtriv = span(|00>) (+) span(|11>) (+) span((|01>+|10>)/sqrt 2); a genuinely different splitting is Vtriv = span((|00>+|11>)/sqrt 2) (+) span((|00>-|11>)/sqrt 2) (+) span((|01>+|10>)/sqrt 2). Both are decompositions of Vtriv into three irreducible (trivial) subrepresentations, but the first line span(|00>) of the first splitting is not among the lines of the second splitting, so the two decompositions into irreducibles are different. This does not contradict Proposition 3.22: the isotypical component Vtriv itself is identical in both (it is the full +1 eigenspace of F), and only its internal basis / line-by-line splitting changed. The source of the non-uniqueness is multiplicity: when an irrep occurs with multiplicity n >= 2, the choice of the n individual copies corresponds to a choice of basis of the n-dimensional multiplicity space, and any invertible change of that basis gives an equally valid finer decomposition. Uniqueness is recovered precisely in the multiplicity-free case.

question: A student claims: 'every finite-dimensional representation of every group can be made unitary by averaging an inner product over the group, so every invariant subspace has an invariant complement.' Explain why the averaging argument requires the group to be finite (or compact, with Haar measure), and give a counterexample: a finite-dimensional representation of an infinite group that has an invariant subspace with NO invariant complement (hence is not unitarizable and not completely reducible).
reference_answer: The averaging argument defines <v|w>_G = (1/|G|) sum_{g in G} <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> (finite groups) or integrates against the Haar probability measure (compact groups). It needs the normalized average/integral to exist and to be invariant under the reindexing g -> gh; for a general infinite non-compact group there is no finite normalization and no invariant probability measure, so the construction breaks down. Counterexample: let G = (R, +), an infinite non-compact group, and define phi: R -> GL(2, C) by phi(t) = [[1, t], [0, 1]]. This is a representation since phi(s) phi(t) = [[1, s+t],[0,1]] = phi(s+t). Consider W = span(e_1), the first coordinate line. W is G-invariant: phi(t) e_1 = e_1 for all t, so W is a (trivial) subrepresentation. Suppose for contradiction there were a G-invariant complement W' with C^2 = W (+) W', dim W' = 1, say W' = span(v) with v = (a, b), b != 0 (if b = 0 then v in W, impossible). Invariance of W' requires phi(t) v in W' = span(v) for all t, i.e. phi(t) v = lambda(t) v. But phi(t)(a, b) = (a + t b, b), and for this to be a scalar multiple of (a, b) we need (a + t b, b) = lambda(t)(a, b); the second coordinate forces lambda(t) = 1, and then the first forces a + t b = a, i.e. t b = 0 for all t, impossible since b != 0 and t ranges over all reals. Hence no one-dimensional invariant complement exists, so W has no invariant complement and phi is not completely reducible; equivalently phi is not unitarizable (a unitary representation would decompose W^perp as an invariant complement). This shows the finite/compact hypothesis is essential: the only G-invariant subspaces of this phi are {0}, W, and C^2, and W cannot be split off invariantly. For finite or compact groups the averaging restores complete reducibility, which is exactly why those hypotheses appear in Maschke's theorem and its compact-group analogue.

question: Part (ii) of Schur's Lemma concludes that a G-equivariant endomorphism of an irreducible representation is a scalar multiple of the identity, under the hypothesis that the field is algebraically closed. Delineate the boundary of this result: show precisely why algebraic closure is needed by exhibiting an irreducible real representation whose equivariant endomorphism algebra (commutant) is strictly larger than the real scalars, and state what part (i) still guarantees without algebraic closure.
reference_answer: Part (i) of Schur (a nonzero equivariant map between irreps is an isomorphism; an equivariant endomorphism of an irrep is 0 or invertible) holds over ANY field, because it uses only invariance of kernel and image. Part (ii) additionally needs an eigenvalue in the field, which is where algebraic closure is essential: without it an equivariant endomorphism may be invertible yet not scalar. Boundary example: let G = Z/4 = <g> act on V = R^2 by phi(g) = R, the 90-degree rotation [[0, -1], [1, 0]]. This representation is irreducible over R: R has no real eigenvector (its eigenvalues are +-i, not real), so there is no proper nonzero real invariant subspace. Now consider the commutant, the real-linear maps A with A R = R A. The rotation R itself satisfies R R = R R trivially, and R is NOT a real scalar multiple of the identity (a real scalar times the identity is diagonal, but R has zero diagonal and nonzero off-diagonal). More fully, the commutant of R over R is {a I + b R : a, b in R}, which is a 2-dimensional real algebra isomorphic to the complex numbers C (with R playing the role of i), strictly larger than the real scalars R I. Thus over R an equivariant endomorphism of this irreducible representation need not be scalar, so Schur (ii) genuinely fails without algebraic closure. What survives from part (i): every nonzero element of this commutant is invertible (indeed a I + b R has determinant a^2 + b^2 > 0 unless a = b = 0), so the commutant is a division algebra - consistent with the general fact (Schur part (i)) that the endomorphism algebra of an irreducible representation is a division ring. Over an algebraically closed field this division ring collapses to the field itself (scalars), recovering part (ii); over R it can be R, C, or the quaternions H (the real/complex/quaternionic types), and this example realizes the complex type.

question: Many representation-theoretic results for finite groups (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthogonality) are proved using the averaging (1/|G|) sum_{g in G}. For compact groups this is replaced by integration against the Haar probability measure. Delineate carefully which statements carry over verbatim to infinite compact groups and which must be modified or fail. In particular address: (a) existence of invariant complements and complete reducibility; (b) finite-dimensionality of irreducible representations; (c) the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and formulas explicitly involving |G|.
reference_answer: The key replacement is: the normalized finite average (1/|G|) sum_g, which is an invariant probability measure on a finite group, becomes the Haar integral integral_G . dg against the unique invariant probability measure dg guaranteed for any compact group (invariant under left and right translation, normalized so integral_G 1 dg = 1). Wherever a proof used only the invariance and normalization of the average, it carries over verbatim with sum replaced by integral. (a) Invariant complements and complete reducibility DO carry over: the Weyl unitarity trick defines <v|w>_G = integral_G <phi(g)v | phi(g)w> dg, which is still a well-defined G-invariant inner product (the integrand is continuous and the measure finite), making phi unitary and giving every invariant subspace an invariant complement; thus every finite-dimensional representation over C of a compact group is completely reducible - verbatim analogue of Maschke. (b) Finite-dimensionality of irreducibles: for FINITE groups every irrep is automatically finite-dimensional (it is a subrepresentation of the finite-dimensional regular representation). For infinite compact groups one must RESTRICT attention or prove a theorem: it is a nontrivial theorem (Peter-Weyl) that every irreducible UNITARY representation of a compact group is finite-dimensional; this does not come for free from averaging and is a genuine modification of the finite-group situation (where it was trivial). (c) Formulas with |G| must be modified or fail: the identity sum_i (dim W_i)^2 = |G| and 'multiplicity of W_i in the regular representation equals dim W_i summing to |G|' involve the finite cardinality |G|, which is infinite for an infinite compact group. The regular representation becomes L^2(G), which is infinite-dimensional when G is infinite; the correct compact-group statement is that L^2(G) decomposes as a Hilbert-space direct sum of all irreducible unitary representations, each with multiplicity equal to its dimension (Peter-Weyl), and the matrix coefficients form an orthonormal basis - but any expression literally equal to |G| is no longer valid. Character orthogonality (chi_i, chi_j) = delta_{ij} survives with the inner product (x,y) = integral_G conj(x(g)) y(g) dg, since it too used only invariance/normalization; however the counting statement 'number of irreps = number of conjugacy classes' and sums over the finite group do not transfer. Summary: averaging-based existence results (invariant complements, complete reducibility, character orthonormality) carry over by replacing sum with the Haar integral; statements relying on the finiteness of |G| (the dimension-squared sum, finite-dimensional regular representation) fail and are replaced by Peter-Weyl, and finite-dimensionality of irreducibles becomes a theorem rather than an automatic fact.

question: For a finite-dimensional representation (phi, V) of a group G, the dual representation (phi^*, V^*) is defined by phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1}. (a) Prove that in a basis phi^*(g) = phi(g^{-1})^T, and that if (phi, V) is unitary then phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)) (the entrywise complex conjugate). (b) Delineate the boundary between a representation and its dual: give the character relation chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations, and explain precisely when V is isomorphic to its dual (self-dual) versus not, giving an explicit example of a NON-self-dual irreducible representation. (c) State what remains true regardless: (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is.
reference_answer: (a) By definition phi^*(g)(L) = L . phi(g)^{-1} for L in V^*. Fixing dual bases, the matrix of the map L -> L . phi(g)^{-1} acting on row vectors is right multiplication by phi(g)^{-1}, which on column-vector (coordinate) representation of V^* is the transpose: phi^*(g) = (phi(g)^{-1})^T = phi(g^{-1})^T, using phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g^{-1}). If (phi, V) is unitary, then phi(g)^{-1} = phi(g)^dagger = conj(phi(g))^T, so phi(g^{-1})^T = (phi(g)^dagger)^T = (conj(phi(g))^T)^T = conj(phi(g)); hence phi^*(g) = conj(phi(g)), the entrywise complex conjugate. (b) Taking traces of the character: chi_{V^*}(g) = tr(phi^*(g)) = tr(phi(g^{-1})^T) = tr(phi(g^{-1})) = chi_V(g^{-1}); for unitary phi this equals conj(chi_V(g)) because chi_V(g^{-1}) = conj(chi_V(g)) for unitary representations (eigenvalues of phi(g) lie on the unit circle, so inverse = conjugate). Thus chi_{V^*}(g) = conj(chi_V(g)). The boundary: V is self-dual (V ~ V^*) iff chi_V = chi_{V^*}, i.e. iff chi_V(g) = conj(chi_V(g)) for all g, i.e. iff the character is real-valued. So real-character (in particular all-real-matrix, e.g. permutation) representations are self-dual, while a representation with a genuinely complex character is NOT self-dual. Explicit non-self-dual example: let G = Z/3 = <g> and let (phi, C) be the one-dimensional irrep phi(g) = omega, where omega = e^{2 pi i/3} is a primitive cube root of unity. Its character is chi(g) = omega, which is not real (omega != conj(omega) = omega^2). Its dual is phi^*(g) = conj(omega) = omega^2, the OTHER nontrivial irrep of Z/3; since omega != omega^2, phi and phi^* have different characters and are inequivalent, so this irrep is not self-dual. (c) Regardless of self-duality, (phi^*, V^*) is irreducible iff (phi, V) is: invariant subspaces of V^* correspond (via annihilators) bijectively and inclusion-reversingly to invariant subspaces of V, so V^* has only the trivial invariant subspaces iff V does. Hence duality preserves irreducibility even when it changes the isomorphism class.
